name: NVLink 1 (Pascal, Tesla P100)
bandwidth_basis: PER LINK, PER DIRECTION. NVIDIA's P100 datasheet (net2-nvidia-p100-datasheet) carries the figure in a chart labelled 'Bidirectional BW (GB/Sec)' with the P100 bar at 160 GB/s against 32 GB/s for K40 and M40, and the spec row reads simply 'Interconnect: NVIDIA NVLink'. That 160 GB/s is therefore the BIDIRECTIONAL AGGREGATE PER GPU, so the per-direction aggregate is 80 GB/s per GPU. Divided across the Pascal generation's 4 links (link-wikipedia-nvlink carries the per-link structure: NVLink 1.0 at 20 GT/s per differential pair, 8 pairs per sub-link, two sub-links per link, 4 links per GPU, total 160 GB/s), the recorded value is 160 / 4 / 2 = 20 GB/s per link per direction. DIRECTION CAUTION: this is the OLDEST record in the family and the only one whose bandwidth comes from a chart rather than a numbered spec field, so the direction reading rests on the chart's 'Bidirectional BW' label. The per-link structural breakdown is still secondary-sourced - NVIDIA's public P100 materials do not publish a per-link rate - so this record is confidence 0.78 rather than higher.
topology: Direct point-to-point links between GPU pairs. With 4 links per GPU an all-to-all mesh is impractical beyond a few GPUs: NVIDIA's own P100 material shows the 8-GPU node as 'up to eight Tesla P100 GPUs interconnected in a single node', reached by grouping the limited links per peer pair rather than by a crossbar.
switching: None. NVSwitch did not exist at this generation - the first NVSwitch silicon shipped with DGX-2 (Volta, 2017 generation), after the Pascal P100. So an 8-P100 node is a partial mesh in which the link grouping dictates which pairs get full bandwidth and which are bandwidth-starved; there is no in-network reduction of any kind.
notes: The first NVLink generation, added 2026-10-03 to complete the 1/2/3/4/5 ladder - the family was missing its starting point, which made the generational trend unreadable. FIRST-PARTY FIGURE (P100 datasheet): 160 GB/s 'Bidirectional BW' against 32 GB/s for K40/M40, i.e. a 5x improvement in interconnect bandwidth, which the datasheet itself advertises as '5X higher performance than current best-in-class technology' for NVLink. NVIDIA's own later retrospective puts the same number at the other end of the trend: the GB200 NVL72 blog (net2-nvidia-nvswitch3-blog) says 'the fifth-generation NVLink is 12x faster than the first generation at 160 GB/s, introduced in 2014', which is a first-party confirmation that 160 GB/s is the correct per-GPU origin figure and that NVIDIA treats it as the bidirectional number. THE GENERATIONAL TREND IS THE POINT, and it is not monotonic in per-link rate: NVLink 1 at 20 GB/s per direction per link, NVLink 2 at 25, NVLink 3 at 25 (doubling the link count 6->12 for its 2x), NVLink 4 at 25 (18 links), NVLink 5 at 50 (18 links), NVLink 6 at 41.7-50 (36 links, contested). NVIDIA roughly tripled the per-GPU aggregate over this span while the per-link rate sat flat at 25 GB/s per direction for THREE consecutive generations - so aggregate fabric bandwidth is link_count x per-link rate, and the link count, not the SerDes, is the lever NVIDIA pulled most often. INFERENCE RELEVANCE: 80 GB/s per direction per GPU against the P100's 732 GB/s of HBM2 means the fabric was roughly 1/9th of local memory bandwidth at this generation, versus roughly 1/7th on NVLink 4's 450 against 3.35 TB/s. The ratio did not improve, which is the structural reason NVLink was not a tensor-parallel fabric when introduced: at 20 GB/s per direction per link the TP all-reduce crossover batch (docs/11-interconnect-decision.md) sits in the low hundreds, so multi-GPU P100 serving was a CAPACITY play - 8 x 16 GB - not a bandwidth play. Direct-attach also meant a partial mesh with no switch, so collective time was set by the weakest pair link.
